By hand. n = 563 / 1094.4 um^2 = 0.51444 per um^2; phi = 563 x pi x 1.150^2 / 4 / 1094.4 = 0.53434. Henderson: Z = (1 + phi^2/8)/(1 - phi)^2 = 4.7763. Pi = n kB T Z = 5.1444e11 m^-2 x 1.380649e-23 J/K x 283.0 K x 4.7763 = 9.600e-9 N/m, i.e. 9.6 nN/m. Only the count 563 gives 9.6 (562 gives 9.5, 564 gives 9.7).

The most tempting wrong answer is 9.3 nN/m, from Z = 1/(1 - phi)^2. Ideal gas gives 2.0; Carnahan-Starling (3D) gives 33.

A check in Python, standard library only:

import math
N, A, s, T = 563, 38.40*28.50e-12, 1.150e-6, 283.0
phi = N*math.pi*s*s/4/A
print(phi, N/A*1.380649e-23*T*(1 + phi**2/8)/(1 - phi)**2)   # 0.53434, 9.600e-9

Sources: Henderson, Mol. Phys. 30, 971 (1975); Thorneywork et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 118, 158001 (2017); Bernard and Krauth, Phys. Rev. Lett. 107, 155704 (2011).
